notes.meaning: God gave Ezekiel this message in the eleventh year of exile, the very year Jerusalem fell to Babylon. Even though the exact month is not given in the Hebrew text, recording the date shows how important the judgment on Tyre was. God wanted His people to understand that the proud nations around them were also accountable to Him.

Tyre cheered when Jerusalem was broken, shouting with delight like someone celebrating the fall of a rival. Jerusalem had sat across major trading routes, so Tyre expected all those merchants and goods to head straight to her own harbors. God notices when people selfishly hope to get rich from the suffering and ruin of others.

The Lord declared that He was standing against Tyre because of her heartless pride. He warned that He would bring many nations against her one after another, just like ocean waves rolling against the shore. The city that built its empire on the sea would face waves of hostile armies crashing over it.

Invading armies would batter down Tyre's defensive walls and smash her watchtowers to pieces. God promised to scrape away even the dirt and topsoil, leaving behind nothing but flat, naked rock. The name Tyre means 'rock,' so God was reducing this boastful fortress down to its bare stone.

Instead of being a bustling center of world trade, the island fortress would become a quiet place where fishermen spread their wet nets to dry. The great city that had enriched itself from many nations would end up as their plunder. God's personal pledge guaranteed that this complete reversal would come to pass.

The smaller mainland villages and towns that depended on Tyre for protection would fall to enemy swords. Because they sat in open country without the island's sea wall, they would be overrun first. When these settlements fell, the people would see that the Lord alone has power over all nations.

God named the conqueror He would send: King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon. He is called 'king of kings' because many lesser kings and kingdoms were subject to his rule. He would march down from the north with a massive force of horses, war chariots, and foot soldiers.

Nebuchadnezzar would attack the mainland villages first to cut off supplies to the city. His soldiers would then build siege ramps and towers against the fortifications to prepare an assault. They would raise a roof of overlapping shields overhead to protect themselves from arrows while digging beneath the walls.

The Babylonian army would slam heavy battering rams against Tyre's strong stonework. Soldiers using heavy iron axes and tools would chop down the city's watchtowers. Human defenses, no matter how thick, cannot hold back God's righteous judgment.

So many war horses would storm the city that their pounding hooves would raise thick clouds of dust over the streets. The rumbling noise of chariots, wagons, and cavalry would make the stone walls shake as troops broke through the breached gates. It paints a terrifying picture of an army bursting into a ruined fortress.

Invading riders would gallop through every street, cutting down anyone in their path. The city's famous pillars, set up as monuments of power or dedicated to idols like Baal, would crash to the ground. Everything Tyre boasted in would prove powerless to save her.

The invaders would carry off Tyre's costly goods and tear down its fine mansions. The passage shifts from 'he' to 'they,' pointing to multiple invaders who would dump the city's stones, timbers, and soil into the water. This was carried out centuries later when Alexander the Great threw the rubble of mainland Tyre into the sea to build a land bridge to the island.

The Lord Himself steps forward to silence the joyful music and celebration in Tyre. The sounds of cheerful songs and harps, which had entertained shoppers and traders for centuries, would be gone. A dead silence would replace the city's worldly laughter.

God repeats that the site would be scraped bare like a rock, useful only for drying fishing nets. The original merchant city would never be rebuilt in its former glory and power. The Lord's own word sealed the lasting end of her greatness.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some critical scholars argue that this prophecy did not come true in every detail because an island city named Tyre was rebuilt and inhabited for centuries afterward.

notes.meaning: The news of Tyre's slaughter and sudden fall would send shockwaves through all the coastlands of the Mediterranean. Trading partners and colonies would shudder when they heard of the cries and groans of the dying. If the strongest city on the sea could fall, no other seaport was safe.

The rulers and wealthy merchant princes of neighboring island nations would step down from their thrones in deep grief. They would cast aside their embroidered robes and sit on the bare dirt, shivering in panic. Seeing Tyre destroyed would strip away all their pride and sense of security.

These foreign rulers would sing a sorrowful funeral song over the fallen city. They would mourn how a famous queen of the seas, whose sailors and merchants were feared everywhere, could suddenly be wiped out. Human renown and military power quickly vanish before the judgment of God.

Distant islands and coastlands would tremble on the day Tyre went down in ruin. They would be deeply disturbed to see this ancient commercial giant swept away into defeat and silence. Her fall reminded every merchant nation that their own wealth could vanish just as fast.

God described Tyre's ruin as being flooded and swallowed by the ocean deep. Great armies would wash over her streets like huge waves, leaving her abandoned and empty like an ancient ghost town. The very sea that once shielded her would seem to bury her beneath its waters.

The Lord described casting Tyre down to the Pit, the quiet world of the dead, to dwell among ancient ruins and peoples long forgotten. While God planned to restore life and glory to His own people in Judah, Tyre would never regain her splendor in the land of the living. Earthly kingdoms sink into the grave, but God's covenant people have a lasting future.

God finished His message by declaring that Tyre's fate would become a terrifying warning to all who hear of it. Though people might look for the grand empire and naval power she once had, they will never find it again. Worldly pride and cruelty finally come to nothing when the Lord speaks.
